newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin rises to opposition challenge over health.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin rises to opposition challenge over health.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, laid low by heart problems, has proved once again that a good challenge is all he needs to put the fight back in him.

After a three-month absence punctuated by a few brief and heavily-edited television appearances, Yeltsin, who announced a month ago that he would have heart surgery, issued a robust response this week to opposition calls for him to resign.
"I said before the elections and repeat now -- don't rush to change the portraits. The country has a president and an active president at that!," he said on Thursday.

His warning, broadcast over the airwaves in the first of a new series of regular radio addresses, sounded more convincing than assurances by his aides that, although in hospital, he was in full control of affairs of state.

They come amid a flurry of meetings with top officials designed to show that he can run the country from Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital, where he is expected to remain until the operation in up to nine weeks' time.

Yeltsin's schedule shows around a dozen meetings in the three months since he disappeared from view in late June after what was later revealed as a likely third heart attack, right before an election runoff against his communist rival.

He has clocked up around half that number in the past week alone, adding the foreign and defence ministers, his chief of staff and security chief to the list, previously dominated by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

On Thursday he met both Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and Chechnya envoy Alexander Lebed, whom he had not seen since his security chief signed a controversial peace deal with the rebels in August to stop 21 months of fighting with the Russian army.

Yeltsin's use of the portraits analogy was clearly designed to remind listeners of the energetic man who steamrolled his way to a second term in the Kremlin with a vigorous, sometimes jokey campaign routine across the vast Russian Federation.

But while his voice came across much more firmly and fluently than at many times in recent months, he is still a long way from the figure who rose to a strong communist electoral challenge and won through at the cost of his health.

His aides say Yeltsin, who used to boast of working 18 hours a day, manages up to three hours with his papers or in meetings. Doctors have ordered him to rest, saying that physical exertion could make an operation too risky to carry out.

Yeltsin's cardiologists have already put off the bypass for around two months from the end of September date which Yeltsin announced when he told Russians about his surgery on television on September 5, his last address to the nation.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, slow off the mark in exploiting Yeltsin's incapacity, has used the delay to issue a steady stream of calls for the 65-year-old president to resign.

He said Russia had been ruled from places other than the Kremlin but never yet from a hospital. "The country itself is gravely ill and requires day-to-day government, decisions on very important matters," he told a news conference on Monday.

Thursday's radio address lasted only six and a half minutes, but Yeltsin covered issues ranging from next year's budget to the shaky peace in Chechnya, stressing that he was in touch with his ministers and giving them orders on a host of problems.
While doctors say he cannot recover his physical strength without an operation, he has shown signs of shaking off the depression which aides hinted had accompanied his ill health.
On Saturday he had a glint in his eye when he warned the West not to expand its NATO defence alliance without Russia's consent in the boisterous tone of the pre-election period.

Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and his younger daughter Tatyana, the key figures in his political life, may have encouraged the latest burst of activity, addressed as much to would-be presidents within the Kremlin camp as those outside.

Chubais has adopted his own analogy to help send the message to any pretenders not to move too soon: "Those who started quickly will have to return to the starting line under the watchful gaze of the referee -- President Boris Yeltsin."
